title: Python Dataclasses: Generated Classes Without the Boilerplate
summary: A study-notes series on Python's dataclasses module: what @dataclass generates, field() and default_factory, frozen/slots/ordering, __post_init__ and InitVar, inheritance rules, asdict/replace, KW_ONLY, and how dataclasses compare with NamedTuple, attrs and pydantic.

chapters.title: Why Dataclasses: The Boilerplate Problem
points: Plain classes need hand-written __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for every simple data holder
@dataclass (PEP 557, Python 3.7+) reads class-level annotations and generates the methods for you
Only annotated names become fields; an unannotated attribute like `tag = 1` is a plain class attribute
Example: `@dataclass class Point: x: int; y: int` gives Point(1, 2) and repr 'Point(x=1, y=2)'
The annotation is not enforced at runtime: Point('a', None) works fine
Decorator returns the same class object, modified in place; it is not a metaclass or base class
Fields are ordered by definition order, which fixes the positional argument order of __init__
Generated __init__ assigns each field to self in order, with no validation
Use dataclass when a class mainly holds data; use a normal class when behavior or invariants dominate
dataclasses.fields(obj) returns Field objects and is_dataclass(obj) checks whether a class or instance is a dataclass

chapters.title: Generated Methods and Decorator Parameters
points: Default generated methods: __init__, __repr__, __eq__
@dataclass(init=True, repr=True, eq=True, order=False, unsafe_hash=False, frozen=False) are the classic parameters
Newer parameters: match_args=True (3.10), kw_only=False (3.10), slots=False (3.10), weakref_slot (3.11)
__eq__ compares fields as tuples and only when other.__class__ is self.__class__, otherwise returns NotImplemented
Setting eq=True without frozen sets __hash__ to None, so instances become unhashable
Hash table: eq=False keeps the inherited object hash; eq+frozen generates __hash__ from the fields; eq only sets it to None
unsafe_hash=True forces a generated __hash__ even for mutable instances, so mutating a key breaks dict/set lookups
repr=False stops __repr__ generation; an explicitly defined __repr__ in the class body is kept, not overwritten
If you define __init__ yourself, @dataclass does not overwrite it (same for __repr__ and __eq__); setting order=True with a hand-defined __lt__ raises TypeError
match_args=True creates __match_args__ so `case Point(x, y):` pattern matching works positionally
Mistake: assuming equality ignores class, but Point(1,2) == (1,2) is False
Mistake: using a dataclass instance as a dict key without frozen=True or unsafe_hash

chapters.title: field(): Defaults, default_factory and Options
points: Simple defaults: `x: int = 0`; non-default fields cannot follow default fields or TypeError is raised
Mutable defaults such as `items: list = []` raise ValueError because the list, dict or set would be shared by all instances
Fix: `items: list[int] = field(default_factory=list)`, which calls the factory fresh for every instance
The check rejects unhashable defaults (list, dict, set); a hashable mutable object slips through since 3.11 rule is by hash
default_factory can be any zero-argument callable: dict, set, lambda: [1, 2], uuid.uuid4, datetime.now
field(init=False) leaves the field out of __init__; set it later in __post_init__ or with a default
field(repr=False) hides a field from __repr__, useful for secrets or large buffers
field(compare=False) excludes a field from __eq__ and ordering; field(hash=None) follows compare
field(metadata={...}) attaches a read-only mappingproxy that libraries can read; dataclasses itself ignores it
field(kw_only=True) (3.10) makes just that one field keyword-only
Mistake: `x: int = field()` with no default still counts as required; default and default_factory together raise ValueError
Class variables: annotate with ClassVar[...] to keep an attribute out of the fields entirely

chapters.title: frozen, slots and Ordering
points: frozen=True generates __setattr__ and __delattr__ that raise FrozenInstanceError
Frozen gives pseudo-immutability: the field bindings are fixed, but a frozen field holding a list can still be mutated in place
Frozen plus eq=True generates __hash__, so instances work as dict keys and set members
Frozen __init__ uses object.__setattr__ internally, which costs slightly more time per instance
slots=True (3.10) builds a new class with __slots__, so instances have no __dict__
Slots benefits: lower memory per instance and slightly faster attribute access; assigning an undeclared attribute raises AttributeError
Because slots=True creates a new class, a zero-argument super() inside methods breaks before 3.14 and the decorator returns a different class object
Slots with defaults: the defaults are stored in __init__ and class dict handling is rewritten, unlike hand-written __slots__ which conflicts with class-level defaults
order=True adds __lt__, __le__, __gt__, __ge__ comparing fields as tuples in definition order
order=True requires eq=True, otherwise ValueError; both instances must be of the same class
Example: sorted(list_of_Version) works when Version has fields major, minor, patch in that order
field(compare=False) removes a field from ordering; reorder fields to change sort priority
Mistake: combining frozen=True with __post_init__ assignment fails; use object.__setattr__(self, 'x', v) there

chapters.title: __post_init__, InitVar and Derived Fields
points: Generated __init__ calls self.__post_init__() at the end if the method exists
Use __post_init__ for validation: raise ValueError for a negative age or empty name
Use __post_init__ for derived values: compute `area` from width and height with field(init=False)
InitVar[T] marks a pseudo-field that is passed to __init__ and __post_init__ but is not stored as a field
InitVar values are passed to __post_init__ as positional arguments in field declaration order
Example: `password: InitVar[str]` hashed in __post_init__ so the plaintext is never saved on the instance
InitVar with a default: the class attribute holds that default value, which is a known quirk
fields() skips InitVar and ClassVar pseudo-fields; asdict and replace also ignore them
Frozen derived fields: set them in __post_init__ via object.__setattr__
Mistake: forgetting to declare the InitVar parameter in the signature of __post_init__ raises TypeError
Mistake: validation in __post_init__ is skipped by replace? No — replace calls __init__, so __post_init__ runs again; mutation after init is unchecked
Alternative to InitVar: a classmethod constructor like from_dict or from_env that returns cls(...)

chapters.title: Inheritance Rules and KW_ONLY
points: Fields are collected from base dataclasses in reverse MRO, then the subclass's own fields are added
A subclass redefining a base field keeps the original position but takes the new type and default
Classic error: base has a default field and the subclass adds a non-default field, giving TypeError 'non-default argument follows default argument'
Fix 1: give the new field a default
Fix 2: kw_only=True on the subclass or the field, which moves keyword-only fields to the end of __init__
Fix 3: KW_ONLY sentinel (3.10), `_: KW_ONLY`, makes every following field keyword-only
Example: `@dataclass class Config: name: str; _: KW_ONLY; debug: bool = False; retries: int = 3`
Keyword-only fields do not affect ordering or __match_args__ positions of other fields
A non-dataclass base contributes no fields; only classes decorated with @dataclass are scanned
A subclass must itself be decorated with @dataclass, or it inherits the parent __init__ without new fields
Frozen and non-frozen dataclasses cannot inherit from each other: TypeError 'cannot inherit frozen dataclass from a non-frozen one'
Generated __eq__ compares class identity, so a subclass instance never equals a base instance with the same values
Tip: put common fields in a base and use kw_only=True subclasses to avoid the default-ordering trap

chapters.title: asdict, astuple, replace and Introspection
points: asdict(obj) returns a dict of field names to values, recursing into nested dataclasses, lists, tuples and dicts
astuple(obj) does the same recursion but returns a tuple
Both deep copy values using copy.deepcopy, so large objects make them slow
asdict(obj, dict_factory=OrderedDict) lets you choose the mapping type
asdict is the usual path to JSON: json.dumps(asdict(obj)) works if all values are JSON types
datetime, Decimal and Enum values need a custom default= function or conversion for json.dumps
replace(obj, field=value) returns a new instance with changed fields; it is the standard update tool for frozen classes
replace calls __init__, so __post_init__ and validation re-run, and init=False fields cannot be passed
replace with an InitVar without default requires passing it again, otherwise ValueError
fields(cls) gives name, type, default, default_factory and metadata for each field; make_dataclass builds classes dynamically
Mistake: assuming replace mutates the object; it returns a copy and the original is unchanged
Mistake: expecting asdict to return the live __dict__; it is a recursive converted copy, and with slots there is no __dict__ at all

chapters.title: Dataclass vs NamedTuple, TypedDict and Plain Classes
points: typing.NamedTuple builds a tuple subclass with named fields, immutable by default, unpackable and indexable
Dataclass is a normal class: mutable by default, not iterable, no indexing unless you add it
NamedTuple instances compare equal to plain tuples with the same values; dataclass instances do not
NamedTuple is hashable and ordered by default through tuple behavior; dataclass needs frozen or order flags
NamedTuple is memory light and fast to create; slots=True dataclass is close, an ordinary dataclass uses a __dict__
NamedTuple has no per-instance field(default_factory), so mutable defaults need a workaround; dataclass supports it
Dataclass supports __post_init__, InitVar, inheritance and field options; NamedTuple inheritance is very limited
TypedDict is a dict at runtime for typed JSON-like data, no methods and no instances of its own type
Choose NamedTuple for small immutable records returned from functions or needing tuple unpacking
Choose dataclass for mutable state, validation hooks and richer behavior
Plain class with __slots__ remains best when you need custom __init__ logic and full control
Table row idea: mutability, hashability, unpacking, memory, defaults, inheritance, JSON conversion

chapters.title: attrs and pydantic: Beyond the Standard Library
points: attrs (third party) inspired dataclasses and is a superset: validators, converters, on_setattr hooks, and slots by default in modern `attrs.define`
attrs.define defaults to slots=True and keyword-friendly API; @attr.s is the legacy interface
attrs validators run at init: `x: int = field(validator=validators.gt(0))`, and converters like `converter=int` coerce input
pydantic BaseModel parses and validates data at runtime from type hints, coercing '42' into 42 in lax mode
Example: `class User(BaseModel): id: int; email: str` raises ValidationError on User(id='abc', email=1)
pydantic v2 core is written in Rust (pydantic-core), so validation is fast, but creating models is slower than plain dataclasses
pydantic offers model_dump, model_validate, model_validate_json and JSON Schema generation, with strict mode for no coercion
pydantic.dataclasses.dataclass gives stdlib-style syntax with validation added
Stdlib dataclass: no dependency, no validation, great for internal data you already trust
Use attrs for rich behavior and performance in libraries; use pydantic at boundaries such as API input, config files and LLM output
Decision rule: trusted internal data uses dataclass, untrusted external data uses pydantic, validators with slots use attrs
Trade-off: each step up adds dependencies, import time and learning cost in return for validation and features

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Gotchas
points: Mutable default list, dict or set raises ValueError; use default_factory
Forgetting that eq=True makes instances unhashable, then putting them in a set
Expecting type hints to validate: Point(x='a') passes silently
Frozen is shallow: a frozen dataclass with a list field can still change via .append
order=True compares fields in order, so field order silently decides the sort key
slots=True breaks super() without arguments before 3.14, and breaks functools.cached_property because there is no __dict__
Default field before non-default field in inheritance raises TypeError; fix with kw_only
Using copy semantics: replace and asdict create new objects; the original stays untouched
@dataclass on a subclass forgotten, so new annotations never become __init__ parameters
Setting attributes in frozen __post_init__ with plain assignment raises FrozenInstanceError
Overriding __eq__ without __hash__ in a frozen class gives inconsistent hashing
Circular or forward references need `from __future__ import annotations` or string types; dataclasses reads annotations lazily as strings

chapters.title: Dataclasses Cheatsheet
points: Skeleton: `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True, order=True) class C: ...`
Decorator flags: init, repr, eq, order, unsafe_hash, frozen, match_args, kw_only, slots, weakref_slot
Mutable default: `field(default_factory=list)`, never `= []`
field() options: default, default_factory, init, repr, hash, compare, metadata, kw_only
__post_init__ for validation and derived fields; InitVar for init-only inputs
Frozen post-init write: `object.__setattr__(self, 'name', value)`
Inheritance: fields merge in MRO order; defaults trap fixed with KW_ONLY or kw_only=True
Helpers: asdict, astuple, replace, fields, is_dataclass, make_dataclass
Hashable recipe: frozen=True with eq=True gives __hash__; mutable plus eq=True gives None
Memory recipe: slots=True removes __dict__ and shrinks instances
Picker: NamedTuple for tiny immutable tuples, dataclass for general data, attrs for features, pydantic for validating input
Rule of thumb: validate at the edges with pydantic, and keep the interior as simple frozen dataclasses
